pages.name: Out of step
pages.text: Lesson 3's scrubber: a voltage wave with a 100 V peak and a dashed current wave with a 10 A peak, in step, as in the heater. Below, the power wave is two humps a cycle, all above the line. Now the current slides 60° late. For part of each cycle the voltage and the current have opposite signs, so their product is negative. The power wave sinks below the line, and that energy flows back to the supply. Its average, the dashed line, falls. Drag the current wave yourself, by its handle.
pages.alt: The scrubber: current 60° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 250 W, Q = 433 var, S = 500 VA.

pages.name: The average
pages.task: At 60° the power wave swings from 750 W down to −250 W. What is its average, the true power?
pages.why: The wave swings as far above its average as below it (the next screen shows why), so the average is the middle of 750 W and −250 W: (750 − 250) ÷ 2 = 250 W. The shaded area above the dashed line matches the gap below it. 500 W is rms volts times rms amps, the resistor's rule, which holds only when the two are in step. 375 W is half the top, lesson 3's rule for humps that start from zero, but this wave dips below zero.
pages.alt: The scrubber: current 60° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 250 W, Q = 433 var, S = 500 VA.

pages.name: Two parts
pages.text: Why 250 W? Split the dashed current into two thinner waves that add up to it, as Trigonometry lesson 8 split the current arrow. One is in step with the voltage, with a peak of 10 cos 60° = 5 A. The other is a quarter cycle behind, with a peak of 10 sin 60° = 8.66 A. The in-step part's power is lesson 3's humps, never below the line. The quarter-cycle part's power is lesson 4's slosh, up and down equally, so it averages nothing. Added instant by instant, they make the power wave.
pages.alt: The scrubber: current 60° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 250 W, Q = 433 var, S = 500 VA.

pages.name: The bench
pages.task: Lesson 6's bench: 20 V across a 6 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω coil in series draws 2 A, with the current 53.13° behind. What is its true power?
pages.why: P = V I cos φ = 20 × 2 × cos 53.13° = 20 × 2 × 0.6 = 24 W. Check it from the resistor alone, the only part that keeps energy: I²R = 2² × 6 = 24 W. 40 W is volts times amps with the angle left out. 32 W uses the sine, 0.8, which gives the reactive power instead.
pages.alt: The bench: 20 V, 2 A, 53.13° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 24 W, Q = 32 var, S = 40 VA.

pages.name: Three powers
pages.text: The triangle names the three. Along the floor is the [[true power]], P, in watts, what the load keeps. Upright is the [[reactive power]], Q, in vars, what flows out and back. The long side is the [[apparent power]], S, in volt-amps, simply volts times amps. P ÷ S is the [[power factor]], here 0.5, which is cos 60°. As the current slides, the floor and the upright trade length while S stays at 500 VA. At 90° the triangle stands on end, lesson 4's coil. At −90° it hangs below the floor, lesson 5's capacitor.
pages.alt: The scrubber: current 60° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 250 W, Q = 433 var, S = 500 VA.

pages.name: The generator
pages.task: A 60 Hz diesel set is rated 630 kVA and 504 kW at power factor 0.8. A load takes 400 kW at power factor 0.6, lagging. How many kVA does it need, and can the set carry it?
pages.why: The power factor is P ÷ S, so S = P ÷ power factor = 400 ÷ 0.6 = 667 kVA. That is more than the set's 630 kVA, so the load draws more current than the set is rated for, though its 400 kW is well inside the 504 kW. A generator is checked against both its kVA and its kW. 400 kVA takes the watts for the volt-amps, leaving out the 533 kvar. 240 kVA multiplies by the power factor, but S is the long side, so it is larger than P, not smaller.

pages.name: Ohms to watts
pages.text: Lesson 6's impedance triangle, R = 6 Ω, X_L = 8 Ω and Z = 10 Ω, multiplied by the current squared, 2² = 4, becomes the power triangle: P = I²R = 24 W, Q = I²X = 32 var and S = I²Z = 40 VA, with the same 53.13° angle. Each part's own meters agree. The resistor's 12 V × 2 A = 24 W, the coil's 16 V × 2 A = 32 var and the supply's 20 V × 2 A = 40 VA.
pages.alt: The bench: 20 V, 2 A, 53.13° behind. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 24 W, Q = 32 var, S = 40 VA.

pages.name: On the mains
pages.task: Lesson 6's resistor and coil in series draw 5 A on 230 V mains. The resistor is 40 Ω, so its meter reads 200 V. What is their true power?
pages.why: Only the resistance keeps energy, so P = I²R = 5² × 40 = 1000 W, the same as the resistor's 200 V × 5 A. Then S = 230 × 5 = 1150 VA, Q = 568 var and the power factor is 1000 ÷ 1150 = 0.87, so φ = 29.6°. 756 W squares only the in-step part of the current, 4.35 A, but I²R takes the whole current. 1323 W puts the whole 230 V across the 40 Ω, which has only 200 V across it.
pages.alt: Lesson 6's resistor and coil on 230 V, 5 A. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 1000 W, Q = 568 var, S = 1150 VA.

pages.name: Hold true power
pages.text: The switch [[Hold true power]] keeps P at 500 W. Now, as the current slides out of step, it must grow taller, so that its in-step part keeps its 7.07 A rms. At 60° the current peaks at 20 A, 14.1 A rms, twice the heater's, while the dashed average stays at 500 W. S grows to 1000 VA and Q to 866 var. A supply cable's heat goes with the current squared, so its bar shows 2² = 4 times the heater's. The current stops at 60° either way: nearer 90° the current needed for 500 W grows without limit, already 27.3 A rms at 75°. Turn the switch off, or slide the current yourself.
pages.alt: True power held at 500 W. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 500 W, Q = 866 var, S = 1000 VA.

pages.name: The motor
pages.task: A motor on 230 V draws 10 A, while its wattmeter reads 1.6 kW. Where has the rest of 2.3 kVA gone?
pages.answer: Nowhere: about 1.65 kvar flows out and back
pages.why: S = 230 V × 10 A = 2300 VA, and the power factor is 1600 ÷ 2300 = 0.70, so φ = 45.9°. Q = √(2300² − 1600²) = 1652 var, about 1.65 kvar, flows out to the motor and back every cycle. None of it is lost, but the cable carries all 10 A to deliver 1.6 kW. Heat in the windings is real power, which the wattmeter already counts, and the wattmeter reads the power wave's average, which is all the motor keeps.
pages.alt: A motor on 230 V mains, 10 A. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 1.6 kW, Q = 1.65 kvar, S = 2.3 kVA.
options: 700 W is lost as heat in the windings
Nowhere: about 1.65 kvar flows out and back

pages.name: Mixed: current ahead
pages.task: Mixed. On the scrubber the current slides 30° ahead of the voltage. Which is true?
pages.answer: P = 433 W and Q = 250 var, leading
pages.why: P = 70.7 × 7.07 × cos 30° = 433 W, and Q = 500 × sin 30° = 250 var, leading, which the triangle shows as −250 var, hanging below the floor. The power factor is 0.87, leading. The power wave still dips to −67 W, because a current ahead is as far out of step as one behind. 250 W uses the sine for the true power.
pages.alt: The scrubber: current 30° ahead. The power wave dips below the line for part of each cycle, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 433 W, Q = −250 var, S = 500 VA.
options: P = 433 W and Q = 250 var, leading
Nothing comes back, as the current leads

pages.name: Mixed: at resonance
pages.task: Mixed. Lesson 7's bench at resonance: 10 V at 50 Hz across 2 Ω, a 10 Ω coil and a 10 Ω capacitor, drawing 5 A. How many vars does the supply provide?
pages.why: The coil's 5² × 10 = 250 var lagging and the capacitor's 250 var leading cancel: the two hand the energy to and fro between themselves. So the supply provides 0 var, P = 5² × 2 = 50 W, S = 10 V × 5 A = 50 VA and the power factor is 1. 500 var adds the two, but one lags and the other leads. 250 var counts the coil alone.
pages.alt: At resonance: 10 V, 5 A. The power wave stays above the line, and its dashed average is the true power. The power triangle: P = 50 W, Q = 0 var, S = 50 VA.
